newsitem.title: USA: GM says IRS seeks more data on Raytheon deal.
newsitem.headline: GM says IRS seeks more data on Raytheon deal.

text.p: General Motors Corp said Tuesday that the Internal Revenue Service has requested more information about the proposed $9.5 billion sale of GM's Hughes Electronics Corp. defense business to Raytheon Co.
GM spokesman John Mueller said GM Vice Chairman Harry Pearce told reporters that questions the IRS is asking about the proposed tax-free exchange of stock are "appropriate."
Pearce said in a breakfast briefing Tuesday that he expected regulatory approval for the deal to be granted in the second half of 1997, Mueller said.
Under the complicated transaction, GM plans to spin off the Hughes Aircraft defense assets to holders of GM Class H stock and Hughes will merge with Raytheon.

Holders of GM, GM Class H and Raytheon stock will receive new shares in the combined defense company, which will retain the Raytheon name. When the deal is done, GM's shareholders will own 30 percent of the company and Raytheon shareholders will own 70 percent.
Pearce defended the deal's tax-free status, saying that it will provide savings for taxpayers by helping to consolidate defense contractors.
Those who have criticized the tax-free exchange ruling as "corporate welfare don't understand the facts" of the situation, Mueller said.

In the same briefing, GM Chairman John Smith said the automaker's relationship with the United Auto Workers union is "pretty good" despite a local strike in Oklahoma City and a series of difficult local negotiations at other plants.
Smith said he believes the union's international leadership in Detroit is not opposed to improving efficiencies that allow cars to be built with fewer workers, Mueller said.

But GM is encountering more resistance to such actions at the local plant level. In the Oklahoma strike, UAW Local 1999 is protesting GM's production of the new Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass cars with about 900 fewer workers than GM used to build previous models at the plant.
UAW President Stephen Yokich is "not going to strong-arm the locals" into accepting reduced employment levels, Mueller said.
